title: B2B video ad examples worth studying
answer: The best B2B video ads to study include Ramp's Super Bowl run, Anthropic's competitor jab, and launch videos from Virio, Gigi and Warmly. Add a handful of consumer classics too: Google's Parisian Love, Nike's Dream Crazy, Old Spice, GoPro, Dove and Blendtec. Each one does one thing really well, whether that's the hook, the story, the humor or the demo, and that principle transfers to B2B.
author: Ademola Adelakun

body.text: How should you study a video ad?

Watch each ad twice: once as a buyer, once as the person who has to make the next one. The first watch tells you whether it works. The second tells you why, and the why is the part you can steal. Copying an ad gets you a worse version of someone else's idea, but copying the principle behind it gets you something built for your buyers.

Every ad on this page is here because it does something specific really well. Some are B2B, a lot are consumer, and that's on purpose. The best B2B creative usually borrows from outside B2B. When you watch, run through the same five questions every time.

items: What's the hook? What happens in the first few seconds that makes you keep watching?
Why does it hold attention after the hook?
What's the structure? Map the beats from open to close.
What makes it shareable? Why would someone send this to a coworker?
How would you apply the same principle to your own content, your buyer and your product?

body.text: What can B2B brands learn from Super Bowl ads?

Super Bowl ads teach you how to earn attention from people who didn't ask for an ad. That's exactly the problem a B2B brand has in a LinkedIn feed. The three below show that a business brand can be entertaining, run a campaign across multiple drops, and even take a shot at a competitor without looking petty.
KitKat: The Heist (Super Bowl)
Ramp: Brian's Party (Super Bowl)

A B2B brand running a Super Bowl ad that doesn't feel like a B2B ad. The Brian's Party series built anticipation across multiple drops before the big game, then Ramp followed it up with a stunt that was even crazier. Study it for the campaign shape as much as the spot itself: tease, release, then top it.
Anthropic: "Can I get a six pack quickly?"

body.title: Anthropic: Can I get a six pack quickly?

body.text: A tasteful example of taking a shot at a competitor. It works as top-of-funnel content because it's funny on its own, and it moves viewers toward the middle of the funnel almost immediately because the joke only lands once you understand what makes the product different.
What makes a B2B product launch video work?

A good launch video makes a complex product feel simple and makes you curious before it explains anything. The three launches below each nail one piece of that: a clear value prop, a "what if" hook, and a LinkedIn post structure that turns a launch into a conversation. If you're planning a launch, pair these with our [video scripting checklist](/playbook/video-script-checklist).
Virio: "The AI Marketer For Enterprise"

body.title: Virio: The AI Marketer For Enterprise

body.text: A clean product launch video that makes a complex AI product feel simple and tangible. Strong hook, tight pacing and a clear value prop. Notice how quickly it gets to what the product does for you.
Gigi: AI for Social Capital
A launch that nails the "what if" hook. It makes you curious before you even know what the product does, which buys it the attention to explain the rest.
Warmly: Marketing Ops Agent Launch

Maximus Greenwald's launch post is a masterclass in LinkedIn product announcements. Bold claim at the top, social proof baked in, and the comments section took off. Study the structure of the post around the video, because on LinkedIn the copy and the video launch together.

body.label: From our own work
body.body: We made the Warmly launch video. It's on this list because the post structure is worth studying, and it's a good example of the kind of launch work we do for B2B SaaS teams. You can see more in the [A2 Media portfolio](/playbook/a2-media-portfolio).

body.text: How do emotional stories sell without selling?

They put the viewer's own feelings at the center and let the brand show up late, or barely at all. B2B buyers are people too, and the story that sticks is the one about them, which is why these three are worth watching even if you sell software.
Google: Parisian Love

Brilliant storytelling through a fixed lens. The whole story plays out inside the product, so you learn what it does without a single feature callout. It's a useful model for SaaS teams with a screen-based product.
BMO: Jane's story

Flips the status quo into a story about possibility by telling the story of what would happen if people didn't tell her what she is and isn't capable of. A bank ad that's about the customer's potential, not the bank.
Nike: Dream Crazy (Kaepernick)

Takes a controversial stance and commits fully. Plenty of people hated it, and Nike's online sales still [rose 31% in the days after launch, according to Edison Trends](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/what-boycott-nike-sales-are-31-percent-kaepernick-campaign-n908251). It's a masterclass in picking your audience and not trying to please everyone. Your B2B version is smaller: pick a point of view your best buyers agree with, even if it puts off people who were never going to buy.
How far can personality carry a brand?

Further than most marketing teams are comfortable with. Old Spice is the proof that personality alone can be an entire marketing strategy, and B2B brands have more room to be funny than they think, because the bar in their category is so low.
Old Spice: "The Man Your Man Could Smell Like"

body.title: Old Spice: The Man Your Man Could Smell Like

body.text: Perfect comedic timing and absurdist humor that launched a thousand memes. It took a tired brand in a dull category and made it culturally relevant almost overnight. Watch how much information it packs in while you're busy laughing.
How do you get customers to make your ads for you?

Make the customer the hero and let their footage, faces or reactions carry the ad. When real people do the talking, the product barely needs to appear. For B2B, this is the logic behind customer stories, and it's a big part of [how many videos it takes to close a deal](/playbook/how-many-videos-to-close-a-deal), since buyers trust peers more than vendors.
GoPro: "Be a Hero"

The product is invisible. All you see is jaw-dropping footage shot by customers. GoPro turned user-generated content into its whole creative engine, and the community makes the ads for them. Study this if you want your customers selling for you.
Dove: Real Beauty Sketches

Real people, real reactions and zero actors. Less than a month after launch it had passed 114 million views and [became the most-viewed online video ad of its time](https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/dove-real-beauty-sketches-becomes-the-most-viewed-online-video-ad-of-all-time-512438111.html), because the insight, that you're more beautiful than you think, is universally human. The product never appears on screen.
How do you make a product demo people want to watch?

Disguise the demo as entertainment and build a format you can repeat forever. Blendtec never explained its motor specs. It just blended things that shouldn't blend, and the demo was the show. SaaS teams can do the same with a recurring series built around a repeatable hook.
Blendtec: "Will It Blend?" (iPad)

Product demonstration disguised as entertainment. It uses curiosity and destruction to make a blender go viral. The series ran for years and never got old because the format is endlessly repeatable. Study the hook structure: same every time, and it works every time.
How do you turn these examples into your own B2B video ads?

Pick one principle per ad, not the whole ad. Take Ramp's multi-drop campaign, Gigi's "what if" hook or Blendtec's repeatable format, and apply it to a single buyer problem your sales team hears every week. Then test it rough before you spend on polish.

If you need a direct-response format to put that principle into, our guide to the [video sales letter](/playbook/video-sales-letter) is a good next read. And when you see a great ad in the wild, save it. A swipe file like this one is the cheapest creative research your team will ever do.

closing.text: Studying great ads is the easy part, and making one for your own buyer is where the work is. See what that looks like for B2B SaaS teams we've worked with.
